## Are users naturally grouped in embedding space?

::: {.takeaway}
We ask whether MovieLens user behavior forms meaningful clusters after
compressing sparse ratings into learned embeddings.
:::

::::: columns
::: {.column width="58%"}
**Not prediction:** we are not evaluating recommendation accuracy.

**Instead:** we test whether learned user representations contain stable,
interpretable clustering structure.
:::

::: {.column width="42%"}
::: {.question-card}
Are audience segments visible in the geometry of user embeddings?
:::
:::
:::::

::: notes
This project is motivated by recommender systems, but the task is not to
predict ratings. The question is whether user behavior contains meaningful
group structure after we represent each user with a learned embedding.
Because there are no true cluster labels, the presentation focuses on
internal validity, stability, agreement, and runtime.
:::

---

## Ratings become embeddings, then clusters

::: {.pipeline}
::: {.pipe-step}MovieLens ratings:::
::: {.pipe-arrow}→:::
::: {.pipe-step}User–item matrix:::
::: {.pipe-arrow}→:::
::: {.pipe-step}MLP embeddings:::
::: {.pipe-arrow}→:::
::: {.pipe-step}Clustering:::
::: {.pipe-arrow}→:::
::: {.pipe-step}Validation:::
:::

::::: columns
::: {.column width="33%"}
::: {.metric-card}
<span class="metric">~1M</span>  
ratings
:::
:::

::: {.column width="33%"}
::: {.metric-card}
<span class="metric">6,040</span>  
users
:::
:::

::: {.column width="33%"}
::: {.metric-card}
<span class="metric">3,706</span>  
movies
:::
:::
:::::

::: {.takeaway}
We compare embedding dimensions of **64**, **128**, and **256**.
:::

::: notes
The data start as sparse user–movie ratings. We convert them into a
user–item matrix, learn dense user embeddings with a neural network, and
then cluster users in each embedding space. The MovieLens 1M dataset has
about one million ratings, 6,040 users, and 3,706 movies.
:::

---

## The MLP creates dense user representations

::::: columns
::: {.column width="52%"}
::: {.compact-list}
1. Build sparse user–item matrix: **6040 × 3706**
2. Mean-center by movie
3. Impute missing ratings with zero
4. Train MLP and output **64D**, **128D**, **256D** embeddings
:::

::: {.takeaway}
Clustering is performed on embeddings, not on the raw sparse ratings.
:::
:::

::: {.column width="48%"}
![](figures/mlp_architecture.png){width="82%"}
:::
:::::

::: notes
The input to the MLP is a 3,706-dimensional user vector. A hidden layer
of size 512 compresses the rating information, and the output layer gives
the final embedding. We trained separate embedding models for 64, 128,
and 256 dimensions to test whether representation size changes the
strength of the clustering signal.
:::

---

## The methods form a 2 × 2 design

::: {.method-grid}
::: {.grid-head}
:::
::: {.grid-head}
**Hard assignment**
:::
::: {.grid-head}
**Probabilistic assignment**
:::

::: {.grid-side}
**Full embedding space**
:::
::: {.method-card}
**K-means**  
Fast baseline; minimizes within-cluster variation.
:::
::: {.method-card}
**Probabilistic distance clustering**  
Soft memberships based on distance to centers.
:::

::: {.grid-side}
**Learned subspace**
:::
::: {.method-card .accent-border}
**Reduced K-means**  
Hard clusters after learning a clustering-relevant subspace.
:::
::: {.method-card}
**Factorial PD**  
Soft clustering with dimension reduction.
:::
:::

::: {.takeaway}
The comparison separates two choices: **assignment type** and
**representation space**.
:::

::: notes
K-means and Reduced K-means assign each user to one cluster. PD and FPDC
allow partial membership across clusters. RKM and FPDC also estimate a
lower-dimensional subspace, which can help if the cluster structure is
hidden inside a smaller set of directions.
:::

---

## No labels, so we triangulate

::::: columns
::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {.metric-card}
**Internal validity**  
Silhouette width and CH index
:::

::: {.metric-card}
**Soft assignment quality**  
Probability silhouette for PD and FPDC
:::
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {.metric-card}
**Stability**  
Bootstrap ARI with 15 replicates
:::

::: {.metric-card}
**Practicality**  
Wall-clock runtime
:::
:::
:::::

::: {.muted}
ARI = adjusted Rand index. Higher values mean stronger agreement between
partitions.
:::

::: notes
Because there are no ground-truth labels, there is no accuracy score.
Silhouette checks whether users are closer to their own cluster than to a
competing cluster. CH rewards compact, separated clusters. Probability
silhouette is used for soft methods. Bootstrap ARI measures whether a
partition reappears under resampling, and runtime tells us whether a
more complex method is worth the cost.
:::

---

## Best overall: RKM on 128D embeddings

::: {.winner-card}
::: {.winner-title}
Reduced K-means
:::

::::: columns
::: {.column width="25%"}
<span class="metric big">128D</span>  
embedding
:::

::: {.column width="25%"}
<span class="metric big">k = 2</span>  
clusters
:::

::: {.column width="25%"}
<span class="metric big">q = 4</span>  
factors
:::

::: {.column width="25%"}
<span class="metric big">0.331</span>  
silhouette
:::
:::::

::: {.winner-footer}
CH index = **139.52**
:::
:::

::: {.takeaway}
This was the clearest evidence of clustering, but the structure is still
only modest.
:::

::: notes
The best selected solution was Reduced K-means on the 128-dimensional
embedding. It selected two clusters and four retained factors, with a
silhouette of 0.331 and a CH index of 139.52. This is the strongest
result in the study, but the value is not high enough to claim sharply
separated user groups.
:::

## RKM gives the clearest separation

::::: columns
::: {.column width="68%"}
![](figures/figure3_best_silhouette_by_method_embedding.png){width="92%"}
:::

::: {.column width="32%"}
::: {.compact-list}
- **RKM leads** in all embedding sizes.
- **128D** gives the strongest signal.
- PD and FPDC are near zero or negative for hard partitions.
:::
:::
:::::

::: notes
This figure summarizes the selected silhouette values. RKM is the clear
winner, especially at 128 dimensions. K-means looks weak here because the
WSS elbow selected four clusters, which had poor separation. PD and FPDC
do not produce strong hard partitions.
:::

---

## Higher complexity only pays off for RKM

::::: columns
::: {.column width="68%"}
![](figures/figure3_runtime_vs_silhouette.png){width="90%"}
:::

::: {.column width="32%"}
::: {.legend-card}
**PD:** fast but weak  
**K-means:** fast, tuning-sensitive  
**RKM:** slower, strongest quality  
**FPDC:** costly without hard-partition gains
:::
:::
:::::

::: notes
The ideal method would be high on the y-axis and far left on the x-axis.
PD is very fast but has silhouette values near zero. K-means is also
fast, but its selected result depends heavily on the tuning rule. RKM is
more expensive, but it is the only method with a clear gain in
hard-clustering quality. FPDC costs more without producing a strong hard
partition.
:::

---

## K-means and RKM recover related structure

::::: columns
::: {.column width="67%"}
![](figures/figure4_average_ari_by_method_pair.png){width="86%"}
:::

::: {.column width="33%"}
::: {.metric-card}
<span class="metric">0.586</span>  
average ARI for K-means vs RKM
:::

::: {.compact-list}
- K-means and RKM find related partitions.
- Pairs involving PD or FPDC are near zero.
:::
:::
:::::

::: notes
Pairwise ARI compares final partitions across methods. K-means and RKM
have the strongest agreement, with an average ARI of 0.586. That means
they recover a related underlying structure. Comparisons involving PD or
FPDC are close to zero, suggesting those methods are finding different
and less reliable partitions.
:::

---

## The two-cluster signal is the most stable

![](figures/stability_all_methods_by_embedding.png){width="88%"}

::: {.takeaway}
K-means and RKM are most stable at **k = 2**; stability drops for larger
cluster counts.
:::

::: notes
The bootstrap analysis compares each resampled partition to the full-data
reference solution. K-means and RKM show the strongest stability at two
clusters, especially in the larger embedding spaces. Stability falls as
the number of clusters increases. PD and FPDC remain near zero, which
supports the conclusion that they do not recover stable hard partitions.
:::

---

## What worked — and what did not

::::: columns
::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {.two-column-card .worked}
**What worked**

✓ Reduced K-means  
✓ 128D embeddings  
✓ Coarse two-cluster structure  
✓ K-means/RKM agreement
:::
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {.two-column-card .not-worked}
**What did not**

✗ PD hard partitions  
✗ FPDC hard partitions  
✗ K-means elbow rule  
✗ Overly complex solutions
:::
:::
:::::

::: {.takeaway}
The useful signal is real enough to reproduce, but not strong enough for
sharp audience segmentation.
:::

::: notes
The strongest evidence comes from RKM, especially in the 128-dimensional
embedding space. K-means supports the same general structure, but only
when we account for the tuning-rule issue. PD and FPDC do not provide
competitive hard partitions in this setting.
:::

---

## MovieLens embeddings show weak but reproducible structure

::::: columns
::: {.column width="33%"}
::: {.metric-card}
**Best model**  
RKM, 128D, k = 2
:::
:::

::: {.column width="33%"}
::: {.metric-card}
**Main signal**  
Coarse two-group split
:::
:::

::: {.column width="33%"}
::: {.metric-card}
**Caution**  
Weak separation and tuning sensitivity
:::
:::
:::::

::: {.compact-list}
**Future work:** spectral clustering, Gaussian mixture models,
HDBSCAN, autoencoder or graph neural network embeddings, and MovieLens
20M robustness checks.
:::

::: notes
The conclusion is intentionally cautious. The embeddings contain some
clustering tendency, but the groups are weakly separated and sensitive to
modeling choices. The next step would be to test methods better suited to
non-spherical or overlapping structure and to use richer representation
learning approaches.
:::
